The house had shrunk.

Claire stood at the end of the driveway, keys cutting into her palm, and tried to reconcile the squat ranch before her with the sprawling estate of her memory. Same color—that particular shade of yellow her mother had called "cheerful" and her father "an eyesore." Same crooked shutter on the upstairs window. But smaller. So much smaller.

She'd driven four hours for this. Left before dawn, coffee going cold in the cupholder, practicing conversations she'd never have with people who weren't here anymore.

The lawn needed mowing. Dandelions had staged a coup along the walkway, their white heads bobbing in the October wind. Mrs. Patterson next door would've had something to say about that. Probably still would, if she was alive. If she remembered Claire at all.

The key stuck in the lock. Of course it did. She jiggled it—up, then down—muscle memory from two decades ago returning like she'd left yesterday. The door swung open onto that smell. Old carpet and Pine-Sol and something underneath, something that might've been her mother's lavender sachets or might've been her own desperation to find anything familiar.

Claire set her bag down in the entryway.

Dust motes spiraled through the afternoon light. The thermostat read fifty-eight degrees. In the living room, furniture sat draped in white sheets like a convention of apologetic ghosts. Her footsteps sounded too loud on the hardwood, so she stopped walking.

Stood there.

Listened to the house breathe.
